content.title: About
content.content: Ginger is the rhizome of the plant Zingiber officinale, native to Southeast Asia. It has a pungent, warming, slightly sweet and citrusy flavor. Ginger is used fresh, dried, ground, and pickled, and is added to tea, soups, sauces, baked goods, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The edible part of ginger is not a root but a rhizome, an underground stem of the plant.
Ginger is related to turmeric and cardamom.
Gingerols give ginger its heat; when dried, they partly turn into the more pungent shogaols.
Pickled ginger is traditionally served with sushi.
India and China are among the largest producers of ginger.

items.title: May reduce nausea
items.content: Ginger is studied as a remedy for nausea, including motion sickness and nausea during pregnancy.

items.title: Contains gingerols
items.content: Gingerols and other compounds in ginger have antioxidant properties.

items.title: May support digestion
items.content: Ginger is traditionally used to ease discomfort and heaviness after meals.

items.title: Anti-inflammatory properties
items.content: Compounds in ginger are being studied for anti-inflammatory effects, but evidence is still limited.

items.title: Adds flavor without calories
items.content: A small amount of ginger makes dishes flavorful with practically no extra calories.

items.title: Heartburn
items.content: In large amounts, ginger may cause heartburn and stomach irritation.

items.title: Effect on blood clotting
items.content: Large amounts of ginger may affect blood clotting; people taking anticoagulants or facing surgery should consult a doctor.

items.title: Gallstones
items.content: Ginger may increase bile flow, so people with gallstones should check with a doctor.

items.title: Supplements and medications
items.content: Concentrated ginger supplements, especially during pregnancy or alongside blood pressure or diabetes medications, should be discussed with a doctor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh ginger can be grated or sliced and added to tea, soups, sauces, marinades, vegetable and meat dishes, and baked goods. The skin is easy to scrape off with a spoon. Much less ground ginger is needed than fresh, and its flavor is different.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh ginger in the refrigerator, wrapped in paper or in a container, where it keeps for two to three weeks. For longer storage, freeze it whole or grated. Keep ground ginger in an airtight jar in a cool, dark place. Discard the root if it becomes soft, shriveled, or moldy.
